segmentation: The segmentation map divides the background into two distinct `person` masks—one for the camera wearer's lower arms and legs at the bottom (3–5 metres away) and one for the opposite person's upper torso and arms at the top (3–5 metres away), who faces away from the camera wearer with their head cropped out of the top of the frame. Between and beneath their meeting hands lies a `dining table` mask representing the manicure table at 3–5 metres, with a small `cup` mask identifying a round white jar on the right side of the table (~3–5 metres from the camera wearer and ~3–5 metres right of the hands), all far away and out of arm's reach of both individuals. The masks clearly trace the contact boundary and mutual occlusion where the camera wearer's right fingers and the nail file overlap the opposite person's left fingertips in the centre of the frame, while across the five frames the camera wearer's left-hand mask pivots from angled left (frame 1) to horizontal (frames 2–3) and back to angled left (frames 4–5). This map makes the exact pixel boundaries separating the two entangled sets of hands and forearms easier to distinguish than in the RGB strip alone. However, it is unreliable in frame 2 where the `dining table` mask disappears completely, in frame 4 where the tape dispenser on the left is misclassified as a `cup`, in frame 5 where the two people's masks merge and swap colours across the camera wearer's wrists, and throughout the strip where the left half of the table and most tabletop tools (bottles, scissors, nail file, phone) go unsegmented.
pose: The pose map renders only 2D hand skeletons in magenta on a black background, showing no yellow body skeletons because both the camera wearer's torso and the opposite person's head and shoulders are out of view at the bottom and top edges of the frame. In the centre of the scene (roughly 3–5 metres from the camera wearer), three hands are tracked far away, out of reach, and out of contact with one another: the opposite person's left hand extending downward from the top-right with fingers spread away from the camera wearer, the camera wearer's right hand reaching up from the bottom-right to support those fingertips, and the camera wearer's left hand reaching from the bottom-left holding the nail file. Across the five frames, the opposite person's left hand stays stationary while the camera wearer's left-hand skeleton rotates inward in frames 2 and 3 to bring the file horizontally across the middle finger before pivoting back to the left in frames 4 and 5. Compared to the RGB image, the wireframe joints make the exact finger flexion, pinch posture, and spatial overlap of the three interacting hands immediately apparent despite heavy occlusion from the nail file and overlapping digits. However, the map is unreliable where it completely misses the camera wearer's right-hand skeleton in frames 3 and 5, fails to detect the opposite person's resting right hand in the upper-left quadrant (~3–5 metres away) across all five frames, and collapses the camera wearer's left-hand finger joints into a tangled cluster during the distant overlap in frame 3.
